WASHINGTON, DC — This week, Reps. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez and Jen Kiggans (R-VA) introduced the bipartisan More Nurses in Rural Schools Act to address the shortage of nurses in the American public school system and ensure students have access to comprehensive, on-site care during the school day. The bill would provide access to student loan repayment for eligible nurses working in schools in health care deserts by opening up the existing National Health Services Corps Loan Repayment Program (NHSLRP) to part- and full-time registered nurses committed to serving schools in health professional shortage areas (HPSA).

While existing student loan repayment programs exist to bring qualified nurses to communities in need, these opportunities typically do not extend to school nurses, who often cannot meet full-time, year-round requirements and do not work in the 2% of public schools designated as School-Based Health Clinic (SBHC) facilities. As a result, registered nurses must choose between working in their communities and taking on the brunt of their student loans, or move to more established clinics. This leaves students without comprehensive services on-site in communities already combatting health care access challenges inflamed by H.R. 1, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which cut health coverage for 31,000 people across Southwest Washington.

The following report, by the NASN, elaborates on the challenges facing school nurses:

Specifically, the More Nurses in Rural Schools Act would eliminate these barriers for school nurses by:

Allowing the Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) to permit an individual who agrees to serve for a time period equal to 2 years or longer as a school nurse in an elementary or secondary school located within a health professional shortage area to participate in the NHSC LRP.

For part-time employees, the Secretary is directed to increase the time period of service to the same number of hours as an individual serving in such a position on a full-year, full-time basis.

Directing the Secretary to establish annual certification requirements for the purpose of verifying the number of hours worked by such individuals.

This follows the application process framework in the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program, which allows states to track these hours as they see fit.

Defining a “school nurse” as “a registered nurse who is employed by a school or local educational agency or State or State educational agency and is qualified under State law to provide assessment, diagnosis, counseling, educational, therapeutic, and other health services to meet student needs.”

In implementation, this bill would help bring comprehensive health care services to elementary and secondary schools across the country in HPSAs – the majority of which are located in rural and partially rural areas.

“Sending your kid off to their first day of school, it’s like your heart came out of your body and it’s walking around in front of you. You want to know your school has every single option they can to take care of kids when they need it.” said Rep. Gluesenkamp Perez. “Letting schools become healthcare deserts isn’t in anyone’s best interest. My bill extends existing loan forgiveness programs to nurses who make the noble choice to serve their community and take care of our children. Especially in rural communities, they’re a priceless lifeline.”

“Every student deserves access to quality health care, regardless of where they live. As a nurse practitioner, I know firsthand how important it is to have a qualified nursing workforce available to care for patients and support their families.” said Rep. Kiggans, “I am proud to join Congresswoman Gluesenkamp Perez in introducing the More Nurses in Rural Schools Act to remove outdated barriers for nurses who want to serve their communities and bring more healthcare professionals to rural and underserved schools.”

“Every student, regardless of where they live, deserves access to a school nurse. The More Nurses in Rural Schools Act is an important step toward addressing persistent workforce shortages and ensuring that students in underserved communities are able to receive the timely, skilled care they need to stay healthy, safe, and ready to learn.” said Lynn Nelson, President of the National Association of School Nurses, “On behalf of the National Association of School Nurses, I thank Representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez and Representative Jen Kiggans for their bipartisan leadership and shared commitment to strengthening school health services and advancing health equity for rural children and families. Their collaboration demonstrates that supporting the health and success of students is a priority that transcends party lines.”

Supporting schools, especially in rural areas, has been a priority for Rep. Gluesenkamp Perez. In 2025, she passed a bipartisan bill to reauthorize the Secure Rural Schools (SRS), recovering $8.9 million in 2024 and 2025 payments for local counties and schools, after it lapsed earlier that year. She has also done extensive work funding and supporting trades education in schools. Recently, she attended the ribbon cutting for a new CTE center at Fort Vancouver High school.

In addition, Rep. Gluesenkamp Perez voted against H.R. 1, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which was signed into law on July 4, 2025. This law eliminated Medicaid eligibility for roughly 17 million Americans–including 31,000 in Southwest Washington. The bill also failed to extend the Affordable Care Act (ACA) enhanced premium tax credits, which helped cover health care coverage costs for lower-income households. Rep. Gluesenkamp Perez co-led the Bipartisan Premium Tax Credit Extension Act to extend these tax credits for one year, giving families more time to make these important health care decisions.

This legislation is supported by the National Association of School Nurses (NASN)

Washington, D.C. – Today, Congressman DeSaulnier introduced the Better Transit for Riders Act, legislation to help transit agencies deliver better service for riders of public transportation by making these systems more efficient and reliable. Specifically, this bill strives to shorten travel times, reduce the number of missed connections, and create a more reliable experience for riders by making it easier for transit systems within the same metropolitan area to coordinate planning, fare integration, service design, and funding strategies.

“Inefficient public transit is not just a transportation issue – it is a quality-of-life issue. Every hour spent tied up in travel and commute time is an hour that could be spent at home with family, socializing with friends, attending to personal tasks, or relaxing after a long day at work,” said Congressman DeSaulnier. “Increasing the reliability and efficiency of transit networks requires transit agencies to raise and use their resources effectively. By bringing together experts across the country, this legislation will help communities learn from successful models and provide their local transit agencies with the tools to better serve riders while ensuring their sustainability.”

“Data is the backbone of transit system safety and reliability across the country,” said Intelligent Transportation Society America President and CEO Laura Chace. “This bill would address ways to improve public transit through better transit data interoperability and technology coordination, and we welcome the introduction of Rep. DeSaulnier’s Better Transit for Riders Act.

The Better Transit for Riders Act would create and convene a task force of transit agencies, local governments, metropolitan planning organizations, labor representatives, community stakeholders, and other experts to develop recommendations and benchmarks for improving transit funding, operations, coordination, and performance. Specifically, the bill would identify best practices related to:

Strategic transit investments and long-term funding models;

Improving the overall rider experience, safety, reliability, and service quality.

Coordination among transit agencies serving the same metropolitan area;

Integrated fares and payment systems;

Regional transit and land-use planning; and

Access to transit and first- and last-mile connections.

This legislation comes as public transit ridership numbers remain around 20% below pre-pandemic 2019 levels nationally, and as Bay Area Rapid Transit (BART) faces a significant financial deficit despite federal pandemic financial assistance and a recent state loan. The Better Transit for Riders Act is intended to increase the standard for transit agencies to increase ridership and bring in more sustainable financing.

The text of the bill can be found here.

DeSaulnier is also exploring avenues for more federal data and oversight of how the nation’s largest metropolitan regions address congestion management and what their biggest challenges are to increasing transit ridership and reducing congestion, particularly post the COVID-19 pandemic. This work would build upon other reports he commissioned from the Government Accountability Office (GAO) related to the positive impacts of telework, which has caused significant changes in commuting trends:

The first report examined trends in telework before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic and how it increased productivity.

The second report laid out data showing the positive impact telework has had on worker productivity and firm performance in certain sectors.

The third report highlights how increases in telework have been beneficial for workers, the economy, and the environment and that more federal support is needed to help localities better plan for and harness the impact of telework.

Today, Representatives Don Beyer (D-Va.), Kweisi Mfume (D-Md.), and Greg Landsman (D-Ohio) and U.S. Senator Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) along with 75 of their colleagues, called on Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) Chair Andrea Lucas to rescind their proposed rule to eliminate protections and strip federal employees of critical civil rights in discrimination complaints. While the lawmakers expressed support for implementing improvements to the existing federal-sector Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) process, they stressed that this proposed rule would make it more difficult for federal workers to challenge workplace discrimination and would weaken essential safeguards for their claims.

The lawmakers were joined in sending this letter by Senators Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.), Tim Kaine (D-Va.), Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), Patty Murray (D-Wash.), Gary Peters (D-Mich.), Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), Mark Warner (D-Va.), and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), and by Representatives Gabe Amo (D-R.I.-01), Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.-03), Nanette Barragán (D-Calif.-44), Wesley Bell Judy Chu (D-Calif.-28), Gil Cisneros (D-Calif.-31), Yvette Clarke (D-N.Y.-09), Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas-30), Madeleine Dean (D-Pa.-04), Mark DeSaulnier (D-Calif.-10), Maxine Dexter (D-Ore.-03), April McClain Delaney (D-Md.-06), Jennifer McClellan (D-Va.-04), LaMonica McIver (D-N.J.-10), Christian Menefee (D-Texas-18), Grace Meng (D-N.Y.-06), Kevin Mullin (D-Calif.-15), Jerrold Nadler (D-N.Y.-12), Joe Neguse (D-Colo.-02), Donald Norcross (D-N.J.-01), Eleanor Holmes Norton (D-D.C.-At Large), Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.-14), Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.-11), Brittany Pettersen (D-Colo.-07), Chellie Pingree (D-Maine-01), Mark Pocan (D-Wis.-02), Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.-03), Andrea Salinas (D-Ore.-06), Mary Gay Scanlon (D-Pa.-05), Hillary Scholten (D-Mich.-03), Lateefah Simon (D-Calif.-12), Adam Smith (D-Wash.-09), Greg Stanton (D-Ariz.-04), Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.-10), Mark Takano (D-Calif.-39), Dina Titus (D-Nev.-01), Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.-12), Paul Tonko (D-N.Y.-20), Juan Vargas (D-Calif.-52), James Walkinshaw (D-Va.-11), and Maxine Waters (D-Calif.-43).

The lawmakers begin, “We strongly oppose the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission’s (EEOC) proposed rule, which would revise the federal-sector equal employment opportunity complaint process. As Members representing hundreds of thousands of federal employees who serve our country every day, we are deeply concerned that this proposal would make it more difficult for those workers to challenge workplace discrimination and would weaken safeguards intended to ensure impartial review of their claims. As such, we urge the Commission to withdraw this proposal and pursue reforms that make the federal-sector EEO process both faster and fairer.”

“We agree that the existing federal-sector Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) process needs improvement. The current process is slow and understaffed, agencies often miss deadlines, and the structure requires an employing agency to investigate allegations against itself. Reforming the process should correct these shortcomings. However, unlike the proposed rule, the reforms should not eliminate protections and shift more power to the agency accused of discrimination,” they continue.

“We urge the Commission to withdraw the NPRM and engage Congress in developing a revised proposal. While speed and efficiency matter, this proposed rule could have the effect of making EEO claims slower on top of stripping federal employees of key rights. The federal government should be a model employer free of discrimination, and its civil-rights process should reflect that obligation,” the lawmakers conclude.

The full text of the letter is available here and below.

Dear Chair Lucas:

We strongly oppose the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission’s (EEOC) proposed rule, which would revise the federal-sector equal employment opportunity complaint process. As Members representing hundreds of thousands of federal employees who serve our country every day, we are deeply concerned that this proposal would make it more difficult for those workers to challenge workplace discrimination and would weaken safeguards intended to ensure impartial review of their claims. As such, we urge the Commission to withdraw this proposal and pursue reforms that make the federal-sector EEO process both faster and fairer.

We agree that the existing federal-sector Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) process needs improvement. The current process is slow and understaffed, agencies often miss deadlines, and the structure requires an employing agency to investigate allegations against itself. Reforming the process should correct these shortcomings. However, unlike the proposed rule, the reforms should not eliminate protections and shift more power to the agency accused of discrimination.

First, the proposal would replace mandatory pre-complaint counseling with direct filing and a substantially more demanding threshold. Under the current framework, a worker generally has 45 days to contact an EEO counselor, who confidentially explains the process and could possibly facilitate early resolution. Under the proposed rule, the worker instead would have 60 days to file a formal complaint to their agency that “must contain sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to state a claim for relief that is plausible on its face.” This not only removes the process for employees to speak with an expert about the process, but it also increases the standard for which federal employees can seek relief and notifies the agency directly of the complaint. Many federal employees are unrepresented and lack access to evidence, such as internal communications, personnel records, or other information that is controlled by the agency. A plausibility screen at the outset therefore risks dismissal of potentially meritorious claims precisely because the agency holds the facts needed to prove them. In fact, EEOC’s own analysis shows that complaints can be erroneously dismissed, as shown by a 30% to 45% annual reversal rate for agency procedural dismissals from 2008-2012. These dismissals occurred even with the lower standard for seeking relief.

The 60 days to file is also shorter than the 180 days granted to legislative branch employees and the 300 days granted to most private sector employees, thus creating a system that disadvantages federal employees compared to other workers.

Second, the proposal would eliminate a federal employee's right to elect an impartial administrative judge proceeding after the agency investigation or after 180 days. Instead, the agency's final decision would become the ordinary adjudication mechanism, and an administrative judge would become available only if the EEOC’s Office of Federal Sector determines that referral is “necessary or efficient” during an appeal.

Administrative judges provide an essential independent check for federal employees concerned about conflict of interest. They take sworn testimony, resolve disputed facts and credibility issues, and assist in developing a complete evidentiary record. Under the proposal, however, an agency would investigate the complaint, decide whether the agency engaged in discrimination, and potentially conduct its own internal hearing. Concentrating these functions in the agency whose conduct is being challenged raises serious concerns about independence, investigatory bias, and conflicts of interest.

Not only is the criteria for determining whether a hearing is “necessary or efficient” vague and burdensome for employees, the proposal significantly underestimates the amount of time required to review an appeal and determine whether it should be referred to the administrative judge. Agency reports of investigations are typically several hundred to thousands of pages; however, the proposal estimate review of these reports will take one-half hour. This timeline is wholly inadequate for the Commission to comprehend that much material and make a complete, unbiased decision on whether a hearing is warranted. This appellate review of a written record is not a replacement for access to an independent hearing and investigation.

Additionally, the proposed rule places the burden on the employee to request such proceedings and explain why they are warranted. The proposal would penalize workers who do not know to request those proceedings by allowing them to be waived if the worker fails to make the proper request. Given that an employee would no longer go through pre-complaint counseling, it could be difficult for the employee to know that they need to ask for a hearing.

The plan would also shift substantial new adjudicatory and administrative responsibilities onto federal agencies at the very moment many lack the personnel and infrastructure to carry them out. The proposal would make the final agency decision the ordinary disposition for every accepted complaint, while requiring agencies to revise procedures; retrain EEO, human resources, and legal staff; update case-management systems; and satisfy expanded tracking obligations. The NPRM does not explain how agencies will absorb these demands, especially amid the Administration’s reductions in force and buyouts that have hollowed out the workforce responsible for implementation. We have already seen the strain agencies’ HR departments are under trying to keep up with routine employee requests and paperwork. In discrimination cases, administrative delays are not harmless inconveniences, but rather significant barriers that postpone meaningful review and, for employees with meritorious claims, relief and accountability. These delays are unacceptable and should not be made worse.

Additionally, the proposed elimination of administrative class complaints would severely weaken the ability of federal workers to challenge systemic discrimination. The proposed rule would permit a worker to assert a putative class claim only for exhaustion purposes and would allow related individual complaints to be processed jointly, but it would prohibit class certification, class notice, class-wide findings, and relief for absent class members. Joint processing is not a substitute for a class mechanism. Administrative class complaints can spread litigation costs, resolve common questions consistently, and provide relief where individual recoveries are too small to make separate cases realistic. Illustratively, in fiscal years 2023 and 2024, $175 million for federal workers was secured through class settlements. Abolishing the process would shift systemic disputes into more expensive federal litigation, increase burdens on the courts, and leave many workers without a practical remedy.

The rule also purportedly seeks to implement the Elijah E. Cummings Federal Employee Antidiscrimination Act of 2020; however, it does so selectively and does not address all of the law’s provisions. For example, the rule does not ensure EEO programs avoid conflicts of interest by being separated from the agency’s HR or General Counsel offices. It also does not address referrals to the Office of Special Counsel (OSC) for disciplinary actions—a critical tool given OSC’s ability to act against those who perpetrate discrimination.

The Commission’s proposed changes are counter to Congressional intent. Congress has found that “[f]ederal agencies cannot be run effectively if those agencies practice or tolerate discrimination.” The Commission’s proposed changes will make it more difficult for federal employees to challenge discrimination and easier for agencies to evade accountability. While Section 717 of Title VII contemplates that federal agencies shall receive discrimination complaints, it also charges the EEOC with effective enforcement of anti-discrimination requirements, including by issuing rules that carry out its responsibility. The current rules, while imperfect, better effectuate these responsibilities by accounting for potential conflicts of interest that may arise from agencies adjudicating complaints. Indeed, by providing federal employees with the right to an impartial hearing before the EEOC, where complainants may have access to discovery and a third-party adjudicator, the current process enables federal employees to have recourse in cases where federal agencies are delaying investigations or appear to be biased in their handling of complaints.

Moreover, Congress established the federal sector administrative process to provide federal employees with a more informal and less-costly mechanism to vindicate their rights. Unfortunately, under the guise of simplification, the NPRM needlessly imposes federal court standards on complaints and eliminates employees’ ability to challenge systemic discrimination, burdening federal courts.

Further, the proposed rule would also make it more difficult for federal employees to obtain legal representation by reducing attorney’s fee awards. The proposal disfavors the use of standard fee matrices, asserts that employment discrimination cases are not complex litigation, restricts compensation for work on unsuccessful claims, and generally allows fees only for services performed after a written complaint is filed. For attorneys who must rely on fee recovery, lower or less predictable awards may make it economically impracticable to accept federal-sector EEO matters. The likely consequence is that more employees will be required to navigate an increasingly technical process without counsel.

Finally, the 30-day public comment period is insufficient for review of such complex changes and is contrary to the Commission’s purported interest in substantive feedback. Notably, the docket shows that the NPRM was withdrawn twice on August 28 before being re-posted on August 31. These technical issues likely caused confusion for stakeholders who sought to submit comments during that time period and ultimately gives stakeholders fewer than 30 days to comment.

We urge the Commission to withdraw the NPRM and engage Congress in developing a revised proposal. While speed and efficiency matter, this proposed rule could have the effect of making EEO claims slower on top of stripping federal employees of key rights. The federal government should be a model employer free of discrimination, and its civil-rights process should reflect that obligation.
title: Beyer, Mfume, Landsman, Van Hollen Lead 75 Colleagues in Pressing Trump Administration to Withdraw Proposal that Would Gut Civil Rights Protections for Federal Employees

WASHINGTON – Today, Representatives Yassamin Ansari (AZ-03) and Dina Titus (NV-01) led 65 House Democrats, including House Foreign Affairs Ranking Member Gregory Meeks and Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi, in urging Secretary of State Marco Rubio to confront Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and the Turkish government over its escalating campaign of repression against LGBTQI+ people, human rights organizations, and advocates.

“The United States must be a leader in defending human rights and what is happening in Turkey demands an urgent diplomatic response. It’s absolutely appalling to see LGBTQI+ people and the organizations that stand up for their rights be targeted by the Erdogan regime,” said Rep. Ansari. “I stand proudly with the LGBTQI+ community here and abroad and will continue to fight for their right to live openly, freely, and without fear, anywhere and everywhere.”

The lawmakers’ letter follows a nationwide operation in which Turkish authorities have detained hundreds of people since September 12, raided the offices of longstanding HIV and LGBTQI+ civil society organizations, restricted access to websites and social media accounts, pursued the dissolution of human rights associations, and arrested organizational leaders and staff on spurious charges. At least 150 people protesting the crackdown have also been detained.

“Turkey’s crackdown on LGBTQI groups and individuals is disgraceful. No person should suffer from discrimination because of who they are or whom they love,” said Rep. Titus, who co-led the letter. “The Trump Administration must restore the United States’s role in promoting LGBTQI rights around the world and punishing regimes like Turkey that persecute people based on their sexual orientation or gender identity. My GLOBE Act does just that.”

The letter is endorsed by the Human Rights Campaign, the Council for Global Equality, and the Planned Parenthood Federation of America.

“Turkey’s attacks on its LGBTQI+ community are a disturbing reminder that the fight for equality and human rights does not stop at our borders. No one should be silenced or detained for simply being who they are or peacefully demanding dignity and freedom. We are grateful to Representatives Ansari and Titus for recognizing that the fight for LGBTQI+ equality is global and that, even amid the many challenges facing our community here at home, we cannot turn our backs on LGBTQI+ people facing persecution abroad,” said Jennifer Pike Bailey, Senior Director of Government Affairs, Human Rights Campaign.

“LGBTQ+ people deserve to be treated with dignity and respect, no matter where they live. Every person should have the freedom to live as their authentic self without fear, stigma, or discrimination. No one should be detained for simply advocating for the human rights and dignity of LGBTQ+ people. We are thankful for Rep. Ansari, Rep. Titus, and their colleagues for urging the State Department to stand up against Turkiye’s attack on health, safety, and basic human rights,” said Caitlin Horrigan, senior director of global advocacy, Planned Parenthood Federation of America.

“Türkiye’s escalating crackdown on LGBTQI+ people and civil society organizations is a direct assault on equality, democracy, and the rule of law,” said Mark Bromley, Co-Chair of the Council for Global Equality. “We are grateful to Representatives Ansari and Titus for their leadership in calling on the U.S. Department of State to stand up for the human rights of all people. Secretary Rubio should use every diplomatic tool available to press for the release of those detained and defend the fundamental freedoms of expression, association, and peaceful assembly. Human rights are not conditional on who we are, whom we love, or where we live, and the United States should make it clear that no one, no matter their sexual orientation or gender identity, will be abandoned when they are under attack.”

“The Erdogan government’s targeted campaign against the LGBTQI+ community and human rights defenders in Turkey is a violation of the core human rights to freedom of expression and association and a disregard for basic human dignity,” said Rep. Mark Takano, Chair of the Congressional Equality Caucus. “Congressional Equality Caucus members Ansari and Titus know the United States can and should do more to protect Turkish people’s freedoms from the human rights violations by the Erdogan government. I’m thankful for their work to put pressure on the State Department to respond to these human rights violations by working to free the wrongfully detained human rights defenders, pressing Turkey to cease efforts to criminalize LGBTQI+ organizations and advocacy, and ensuring human rights are integrated into all bilateral engagements.”

Ansari’s letter is co-signed by Representatives Gabe Amo (RI-01), Becca Balint (VT), Nanette Barragán (CA-44), Wesley Bell (MO-01), Everton Blair, Jr. (GA-13), Julia Brownley (CA-26), Salud Carbajal (CA-24), Joaquin Castro (TX-20), Angie Craig (MN-02), Jasmine Crockett (TX-30), Danny Davis (IL-07), Diana DeGette (CO-01), Mark DeSaulnier (CA-10), Maxine Dexter (OR-03), Lois Frankel (FL-22), Maxwell Frost (FL-10), Robert Garcia (CA-42), Sylvia Garcia (TX-29), Daniel Goldman (NY-10), Josh Gottheimer (NJ-05), Adelita Grijalva (AZ-07), Jonathan Jackson (IL-01), Sara Jacobs (CA-51), Pramila Jayapal (WA-07), Julie Johnson (TX-32), Sydney Kamlager-Dove (CA-37), William Keating (MA-09), Ro Khanna (CA-17), Raja Krishnamoorthi (IL-08), Greg Landsman (OH-01), John Larson (CT-01), Teresa Leger Fernandez (NM-03), Sam Liccardo (CA-16), Ted Lieu (CA-36), Zoe Lofgren (CA-18), Stephen Lynch (MA-08), Sarah McBride (DE), James McGovern (MA-02), Gregory Meeks (NY-05), Grace Meng (NY-06), Jared Moskowitz (FL-23), Kevin Mullin (CA-15), Jerrold Nadler (NY-12), Eleanor Norton (DC), Chris Pappas (NH-01), Nancy Pelosi (CA-11), Mark Pocan (WI-02), Mike Quigley (IL-05), Emily Randall (WA-06), Jamie Raskin (MD-08), Andrea Salinas (OR-06), Janice Schakowsky (IL-09), Bradley Schneider (IL-10), Melanie Stansbury (NM-01), Greg Stanton (AZ-04), Haley Stevens (MI-11), Mark Takano (CA-39), Shri Thanedar (MI-13), Dina Titus (NV-01), Paul Tonko (NY-20), Norma Torres (CA-35), Ritchie Torres (NY-15), Debbie Wasserman Schultz (FL-25), and Bonnie Watson Coleman (NJ-12).

Read the letter HERE and below.

Dear Secretary Rubio,

We are writing to express grave concerns regarding President Erdogan and the Turkish government’s alarming campaign of repression against LGBTQI+ people, human rights organizations, and advocates in a recent nationwide operation.

In recent years, we have witnessed an increasingly systematic effort to restrict the human rights and civic participation of LGBTQI+ people in Turkey. The Turkish government has invoked so-called “family values” and “public morality” to justify restrictions on freedom of expression, association, and peaceful assembly, while courts and prosecutors have increasingly relied on vague provisions concerning obscenity and public morality to target LGBTQI+ people, human rights defenders, civil society organizations, and journalists. Authorities have repeatedly banned and violently dispersed Pride gatherings, individuals have faced prosecution for defending human rights, and government officials have escalated anti-LGBTQI+ rhetoric.

This latest crackdown represents a dangerous and significant escalation of that broader campaign. Since September 12, 2026, Turkish authorities have detained hundreds of people, raided the offices of longstanding and trusted HIV and LGBTQI+ civil society organizations, restricted access to websites and social media accounts, and pursued dissolution proceedings against human rights associations. Leadership and staff of LGBTQI+ human rights organizations have been arrested under spurious charges. In addition, Turkish authorities recently detained at least 150 people who were protesting this most recent anti-LGBTQI+ crackdown. Together, these developments mark a dangerous new phase in the Erdogan regime’s efforts to use criminal law and the state apparatus to suppress legitimate human rights advocacy on behalf of the LGBTQI+ community.

The Turkish government’s actions directly violate international human rights frameworks to which Turkey is a signatory, including the European Convention on Human Rights and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, to which the United States is party. They also are an affront to basic human dignity and the values expected of a fellow NATO member, an alliance founded on shared democratic principles, including individual liberty, human freedom, and the right to peaceful assembly.

These developments warrant an urgent diplomatic response from the United States to protect the rights of freedom of expression, association, and assembly for all Turkish citizens, regardless of their sexual orientation or gender identity. We therefore urge you to use all available channels to raise these concerns directly with the Turkish government; press for the immediate release of those arrested and detained for their legitimate human rights activities; and ensure that the U.S. Embassy in Ankara closely monitors related judicial proceedings. We further urge the Department to press Turkish authorities to cease efforts to criminalize LGBTQI+ organizations and advocacy and to affirm the right of all people to peacefully assemble.

We also request an update on the Department’s broader strategy for addressing human rights with the Turkish government. While the current crackdown on LGBTQI+ people and civil society demands urgent attention, it must be seen as part of a broader pattern of human rights violations and democratic backsliding in Turkey. We urge the Department to ensure that human rights are meaningfully integrated into all bilateral engagements and request a clear explanation of how the Department intends to do so.

Defending the rights of LGBTQI+ individuals around the globe is imperative for international peace and stability, the flourishing of liberal democracy, and the protection of the rule of law. As you yourself have noted, “We should never, ever tolerate human rights violations against any person for their political views, their religious beliefs, or their sexual orientation.” The United States must hold true to that principle in its engagement with the Turkish government.

Thank you for your attention to this critical matter. We look forward to your prompt response no later than October 30, 2026.

Sincerely,

Yassamin Ansari

Member of Congress

Follow @RepYassAnsari on all social media platforms and visit Ansari.House.gov to learn more.

Congressman Chris Pappas (NH-01), Congressman Jerry Nadler (NY-12), and Congresswoman Maggie Goodlander (NH-02) announced they led 50 members of the House in calling for U.S. Secretary of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) Scott Turner to release the delayed Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) for Housing Opportunities for Persons with AIDS (HOPWA) grants and urged the Department to immediately expedite the process of awarding grant funding for the HOPWA program. The call comes as organizations across the nation are at risk of losing critical HOPWA funding that they rely on to serve those with HIV/AIDS. Many previously awarded HUD grants are expiring today, September 30, yet HUD has not released a NOFO nor communicated with grantee organizations who are relying on the renewal of their awards to continue providing critical housing and health care services to communities across the nation. The call is part of a bipartisan, bicameral effort led by U.S. Senator Jeanne Shaheen.

The lawmakers wrote, in part: “We write to express our grave concerns regarding the delayed Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) for the Housing Opportunities for Persons with AIDS (HOPWA) program. For many organizations in our communities, this program is vital to ensuring individuals with HIV/AIDS have access to safe and stable housing. We urge you to release the NOFO immediately and expedite the awards so communities can continue to provide support and housing to those who need it.”

They continued: “Unfortunately, many competitive HOPWA awards will expire tomorrow on September 30, 2026. Your department still has not released a NOFO, and grantees have received no information regarding the renewal of their awards. HOPWA is the only Federal program dedicated to the housing needs of people living with HIV/AIDS, making any gap in funding detrimental for the organizations providing support and the individuals and communities that depend on this program.”

The lawmakers concluded: “We understand that the awarding process takes careful review, but because these applicants are all seeking renewals, they have already been vetted and approved by your department. We urge you to expedite this process immediately and release awards as soon as possible. Without these critical funds, individuals with HIV/AIDS will face the risk of homelessness, and the organizations that help them may have to close their doors.”

Over 30 percent of those with HIV are living below the poverty line, and 20 percent have experienced homelessness in recent years. As the only HUD program dedicated to housing support for those with HIV/AIDS, expiration of previous awards and a delayed grant process by HUD could lead to staff layoffs and cuts to health care and housing services—exacerbating homelessness for some of the country’s most vulnerable communities.

The full letter can be read here.

Members of the House signing the letter were Representatives Jasmine Crockett (TX-30), Betty McCollum (MN-04), Adriano Espaillat (NY-13), Mark Pocan (WI-02), Eleanor Holmes Norton (DC-AL), Kevin Mullin (CA-15), Dan Goldman (NY-10), Jonathan Jackson (IL-01), Rashida Tlaib (MI-12), Wesley Bell (MO-01), Gwen Moore (WI-04), Danny Davis (IL-07), Joyce Beatty (OH-03), Ro Khanna (CA-17), Bennie Thompson (MS-02), Yassamin Ansari (AZ-03), Mark DeSaulnier (CA-10), Robert Garcia (CA-42), Bonnie Watson Coleman (NJ-12), Haley Stevens (MI-11), Everton Blair (GA-13), Seth Moulton (MA-06), Judy Chu (CA-28), Julie Johnson (TX-32), Pramila Jayapal (WA-07), Mike Quigley (IL-05), Nancy Pelosi (CA-11), Troy Carter (LA-02), Adelita Grijalva (AZ-07), Lateefah Simon (CA-12), Frederica Wilson (FL-24), Delia Ramirez (IL-03), Nydia Velázquez (NY-07), Sean Casten (IL-06), Raja Krishnamoorthi (IL-08), Gabe Vasquez (NM-02), Joe Courtney (CT-02), Paul Tonko (NY-20), Bill Foster (IL-11), Diana DeGette (CO-01), Stephen Lynch (MA-08), Robin Kelly (IL-02), Nikema Williams (GA-05), Josh Gottheimer (NJ-05), William Keating (MA-09), Val Hoyle (OR-04), Maxwell Frost (FL-10), Terri Sewell (AL-07), Angie Craig (MN-02) and Juan Vargas (CA-52).

HOUSTON, TX — A bipartisan coalition of the Texas congressional delegation is speaking with one voice on where the United States Space Academy belongs: Texas.

Today, Rep. Christian D. Menefee (TX-18) led a coalition of Democratic members of the Texas delegation in sending a letter to the Presidential Commission on the United States Space Academy, urging the Commission to locate the new institution in Texas. The letter adds Democratic support to a case that Republican members of the delegation have also publicly championed in recent weeks, uniting Texans across party lines behind the state's bid.

Texas is home to NASA's Johnson Space Center, which has trained every American astronaut and run Mission Control for more than sixty years. It is home to the only state where the full space industry, developing, building, testing, launching, and operating spacecraft, comes together in one place. And it is home to a network of universities and research institutions, from the University of Texas System to Texas A&M, already training the engineers and scientists the Academy will need.

The Democratic letter also points to Texas's role as the energy capital of the world and the skilled workforce that comes with it, along with the state's rapidly growing and diverse population as an asset for the Academy's future student body.

"Texas has the history, the infrastructure, and the workforce this Academy needs on day one," said Congressman Menefee. "That is true regardless of party, and it is why members from across the Texas delegation are making the same case to the Commission."

The letter was co-signed by Reps. Henry Cuellar (TX-28), Joaquin Castro (TX-20), Marc Veasey (TX-33), Lizzie Fletcher (TX-07), Veronica Escobar (TX-16), Sylvia Garcia (TX-29), Jasmine Crockett (TX-30), Vicente Gonzalez (TX-34), Greg Casar (TX-35), Lloyd Doggett (TX-37), and Julie Johnson (TX-32).

Texas is competing against several other states, including Alabama, Colorado, and Florida, to host the Academy. The Presidential Commission is expected to use responses to its Request for Information, due October 26, to help select a permanent location, with a goal of breaking ground by 2027 and welcoming its first class of students in 2028.

Click HERE to read the full letter.
title: Bipartisan Texas Delegation Unites Behind Bid to Bring U.S. Space Academy to Texas

San Diego, CA – Last week, U.S. Representative Scott Peters (CA-50) hosted a virtual training event with Rep. Juan Vargas (CA-52) and representatives from Kids Belong in Classrooms and Immigrant Defenders Law Center. The webinar helped ensure community members understand how to safely interact with federal law enforcement officers, what to do if they or their loved ones are detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and what resources are available to San Diego’s immigrant community.

During the week of September 7th, San Diego Unified School District (SDUSD) and San Diego City College both informed the Congressman's office of ICE arrest activity outside their schools. These are in addition to a dramatic increase in ICE activity across San Diego County, especially around sensitive locations like schools, childcare facilities, hospitals, courthouses, and places of worship.

“Regardless of your immigration status, you have certain rights in this country,” said Rep. Peters. “These resources are more important than ever as community members continue to navigate frightening and lawless interactions with federal law enforcement officers under the Trump Administration. Until ICE operations change to responsibly target dangerous criminals instead of hardworking families, I will continue to push for real reforms and hold the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) accountable for the fear it has inflicted on my constituents and communities across the country.”

“Everyone has constitutional rights when interacting with ICE or law enforcement – regardless of immigration status. As ICE continues to target our communities, it’s more important than ever that people know their rights and understand how to exercise them,” said Rep. Juan Vargas. “Thank you to my colleague, Rep. Scott Peters, for holding this important Know Your Rights training to help us look out for one another.”

Watch and share a recording of the training here. Additional resources from Kids Belong in Classrooms and Immigrant Defenders Law Center can be accessed below:

Toolkit for Organizing in Your School Community

Spanish Kids Belong in Classrooms Toolkit

BOSTON, MA – Today, Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley (MA-07) and Congressman Eugene Vindman (VA-07) introduced the Wigs for Warriors Act, legislation that would require TRICARE to cover cranial prostheses for individuals with alopecia areata and other non-cancer conditions that cause permanent or medically documented hair loss.

“When individuals in our military families experience severe hair loss, they should be met with the support and care they need to feel like their authentic selves,” said Rep. Pressley. “Through my own experience with alopecia areata, I understand the psychological, social, and economic impact that comes with navigating severe hair loss—and I know that we can do something to lighten the load. For some, accessing medical-grade wigs can make all the difference. That’s why I’m proud to lead the Wigs for Warriors Act alongside Rep. Vindman and bring much-deserved relief and support to TRICARE beneficiaries with alopecia areata and other hair loss conditions.”

“I heard directly from a constituent, a 16-year-old from Prince William County and daughter of a U.S. Marine, who lost all of her hair to alopecia areata by the end of second grade. She told my team how a medical-grade wig could have helped her navigate the emotional and social challenges of losing her hair, but that these wigs can be incredibly expensive,” said Vindman. “This bill, which I am proud to lead alongside Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley, will help ensure TRICARE beneficiaries with alopecia areata, like my constituent, have access to the care and support they need to feel comfortable and confident.”

TRICARE, the insurance for servicemembers and military families, has extremely limited coverage for individuals experiencing severe hair loss. Currently, patients with alopecia areata receive no coverage for a cranial prosthesis — a medical-grade, custom-fitted wig designed to address medically related hair loss.

The bill would require TRICARE to cover cranial prostheses for individuals with alopecia areata and other non-cancer conditions that cause permanent or medically documented hair loss, as certified by a physician. Coverage would also extend to hair loss resulting from chemotherapy, regardless of the underlying condition being treated.

The legislation would also eliminate TRICARE’s current lifetime limit of one prosthesis per patient, allowing cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy to receive coverage for multiple wigs as medically necessary.

The Wigs for Warriors Act is supported by the National Alopecia Areata Foundation (NAAF).

“The National Alopecia Areata Foundation applauds the introduction of the Wigs for Warriors Act of 2026 and thanks Representative Vindman for his efforts to improve the lives of members of the military and their families living with the autoimmune disease alopecia areata,” said Ryan Reczek, President & CEO of the National Alopecia Areata Foundation. “This legislation is critical to ensure that medically necessary cranial prostheses, also known as medical wigs, that are used to restore well-being and support mental health, are affordable and accessible under TRICARE.”

“This act is life changing for both the military and medical hair loss communities, allowing for better mental health of our service members and their families,” said a 16-year-old resident of Prince William County with alopecia areata. “Representative Vindman and his team not only took the time to listen to my story but have moved forward to resolving the issue. I am forever grateful.”

Text of the bill can be accessed here.

BACKGROUND

Alopecia areata is a common autoimmune disease that causes the immune system to attack a person’s hair follicles, resulting in patchy or complete hair loss across the scalp and body. Nearly 6.7 million people in the United States are directly affected by alopecia areata, with about 700,000 currently living with active disease. The remaining millions have had the disease or will likely develop it at some point.

Alopecia areata carries a substantial mental health burden and wigs are a documented, effective way to manage it. The psychological impact of alopecia areata can be profound, with elevated rates of anxiety and depression, increased time off work, and impaired quality of life, stemming largely from the fact that hair plays a crucial role in shaping an individual’s identity, self-esteem, and social interactions. This burden is especially acute for young people who develop the condition.

Congresswoman Pressley has been steadfast in her advocacy for women’s health, ending race-based hair discrimination, and introducing policies that affirm the right of women to show up in the world as their full, authentic selves.

On March 18, 2026, Congresswoman Pressley, alongside Congresswoman Bonnie Watson Coleman (NJ-12) and Congresswoman Jennifer McClellan (VA-04) reintroduced the Recognition of Traction Alopecia in Service Women Act, legislation that would support and expand medical coverage of traction alopecia in the military.

Rep. Pressley is a lead co-sponsor of the Creating a Respectful and Open World for Natural Hair (CROWN) Act, legislation with Reps. Bonnie Watson Coleman (NJ-12), Gwen Moore (WI-04), Barbara Lee (CA-13) and Ilhan Omar (MN-05) that would ban discrimination based on hair textures and hairstyles that are commonly associated with a particular race or national origin.

Congresswoman Pressley, alongside Congresswomen Brown and Velázquez, have led congressional efforts to ban formaldehyde in hair products. In March 2026, Rep. Pressley, alongside Congresswoman Shontel Brown (OH-11) and Congresswoman Nydia Velázquez (NY-07), introduced the Health Hair Act, legislation to effectively ban formaldehyde from hair products. Last year, they sent a letter to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) requesting an update on delays in implementation of a rule to ban formaldehyde and other formaldehyde-releasing chemicals in hair products. In October 2023, the FDA proposed the ban of formaldehyde in hair products following a letter led by Reps. Pressley and Brown, which called on the agency to investigate the health risks associated with the chemical. However, the implementation of the ban has continuously been delayed.

In February 2026, Rep. Pressley, alongside Rep. Jim McGovern (MA-02) and Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), led their colleagues in re-introducing the Wigs as Durable Medical Equipment Act, legislation to help individuals affected by Alopecia Areata and patients with cancer who are undergoing chemotherapy by allowing medical wigs and other head coverings to be covered under the Medicare program.

Rep. Pressley leads the Anti-Racism in Public Health Act, a bicameral bill to declare structural racism a public health crisis and confront its public health impacts through two bold new programs within the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Rep. Pressley originally introduced the bill in September 2020.

In 2020, the House passed an amendment introduced by Congresswoman Pressley to provide $5 million dollars for the National Institutes of Health’s National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases to fund research on the causes, impacts, and possible treatments of Alopecia areata.

In December 2019, Rep. Pressley and her colleagues sent a letter to Johnson & Johnson Chairman and CEO Alex Gorsky seeking information on the targeted marketing and sale of the company’s talc-based baby powder and its potential to cause harm, particularly to women, teenage girls, and people of color, due to asbestos contamination.

Washington, D.C. – Today, Congressman Bennie G. Thompson (MS-02) issued the following statement following notification from the National Credit Union Administration (NCUA) that Jackson Area Federal Credit Union (JAFCU) has been liquidated and that Five Star Credit Union has assumed its member share accounts:

“Jackson Area Federal Credit Union has served thousands of families, public employees, and members of the Jackson and Hinds County communities for decades. The liquidation of this longstanding institution is a serious development, and my primary concern remains protecting the members who entrusted their hard-earned money to this credit union.

“NCUA has assured my office that members transferring to Five Star Credit Union will experience no interruption in service and that federally insured accounts remain protected through the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund. Members deserve a transition that is orderly, transparent, and protects their access to their money.

“While protecting members must come first, the liquidation of Jackson Area Federal Credit Union also raises serious questions about the circumstances that brought the institution to this point. My office will continue engaging with NCUA to ensure there is full transparency and accountability regarding what occurred, how members were affected, and what steps are being taken to protect them moving forward.”

On September 30, NCUA facilitated a partial purchase and assumption agreement under which Five Star Credit Union purchased certain JAFCU assets and assumed its member share accounts. NCUA subsequently liquidated JAFCU.
title: Congressman Thompson Responds to Liquidation of Jackson Area Federal Credit Union

U.S. Congressman Everton Blair Introduces Legislation to Bring Deported U.S. Army Veteran Godfrey Oliver Wade Home
Media Contact:
Allison Phipps, Allison.Phipps@mail.house.gov ; Amya Enlow, Amya.Enlow@mail.house.gov
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, U.S. Congressman Everton Blair (GA-13), introduced a bill for the relief of Godfrey Oliver Wade, a Jamaican-born U.S. Army veteran and Covington, Georgia resident who was deported in February 2026 after living in the United States for more than 50 years. The legislation seeks to grant Mr. Wade lawful status, allowing him to return home to his children, grandchildren and the nation he has served with distinction.
Mr. Wade entered the United States lawfully in 1975 as a teenager and has called the nation home ever since. He went on to enlist in the U.S. Army, serving four years on active duty, including three years overseas supporting vital operations during the final years of the Cold War, before receiving an honorable discharge.
Despite his decorated military service and deep ties to the community, Mr. Wade was held in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody for nearly five months. He was deported earlier this year after an emergency stay of removal was denied, even while an appeal in his case remained pending.
"Godfrey Wade answered the call of service, enlisting in the U.S. Army, leaving behind a legacy of honorably protecting our nation," said Congressman Blair. "For over half a century, he built his life here as a lawful permanent resident, a father, and a grandfather. To deport an honorably discharged veteran while his legal appeals were still pending is a profound injustice. He fought for our country, so now it is time for us to fight for him and bring him home."
The relief bill would pave the way for Mr. Wade's immediate return to the United States and restore his status as a permanent resident.
###
title: U.S. Congressman Everton Blair Introduces Legislation to Bring Deported U.S. Army Veteran Godfrey Oliver Wade Home

This week, the U.S. Senate passed H.R. 1190, Congresswoman Janelle Bynum’s (OR-05) bipartisan Expanding Access to Capital for Rural Job Creators Act. The legislation would help rural small businesses overcome barriers to accessing capital.

The bill updates the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 by requiring the SEC’s Office of the Advocate for Small Business Capital Formation to report annually on the unique challenges rural businesses face when seeking investment. These reports will give Congress better information as it considers ways to improve access to capital for rural job creators.

"Rural small businesses shouldn’t have to work twice as hard just because of their ZIP code,” said Congresswoman Janelle Bynum. “The Senate passing this bill gets us one step closer to changing that. Rural entrepreneurs have the ideas and the hustle. They deserve a fair shot to grow them into something bigger."

“Rural small businesses are essential to communities across Montana, but too many still face unnecessary barriers when trying to access capital,” said Congressman Troy Downing (MT-02), the bill’s co-lead. “I’m proud of our legislation, which will help make sure rural businesses are no longer overlooked when Congress considers how to expand access to capital and support job creation.”

Senator John Kennedy (R-LA.) led the U.S. Senate companion bill to passage.

“Rural small businesses are the backbone of many communities across America, but too many face challenges accessing capital. I’m glad the Senate passed our bill to make sure Congress understands those challenges and help rural job creators grow their businesses, create jobs and serve their communities,” said Senator Kennedy.

Read the bill HERE.

Background:

The SEC’s Office of the Advocate for Small Business Capital Formation is required to identify problems that small businesses face when securing access to capital and submit an annual report to Congress.

Currently, the Office’s list of applicable entities are minority-owned, women-owned, and disaster-stricken small businesses.

This legislation would require the SEC’s Office of the Advocate for Small Business Capital Formation to add rural small businesses to its list of applicable entities.

Kamlager-Dove, Bacon Reintroduce Bipartisan Bills to Expand Medicaid Eligibility for Foster Youth
WASHINGTON, DC — Today, Foster Youth Caucus Co-Chairs Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-CA) and Rep. Don Bacon (R-NE) reintroduced a legislative package to promote greater health equity by expanding Medicaid eligibility for foster youth.  
The Foster Youth Dental Act of 2026 would expand Medicaid eligibility for foster youth by providing more incentives for dental providers, increasing Medicaid enrollment opportunities, and preventing lapses in coverage.  
The Expanding Coverage for Former Foster Youth Act would broaden Medicaid-to-26 eligibility for former foster youth by removing enrollment restrictions, including those who exited to kinship guardianships or emancipated before 18, and requiring states to conduct coordinated outreach and enrollment efforts. 
“We must support the health care needs of the more than 23,000 young people who age out of our nation’s foster care system each year,” said Rep. Kamlager-Dove. “I’m proud to reintroduce these bipartisan, compassionate bills alongside Rep. Bacon to close persistent gaps in our health care system that too often force foster youth to go without the care they deserve. As Co-Chair of the Foster Youth Caucus, I remain committed to working across the aisle to ensure every foster youth has access to the resources they need, from health care to education, employment, and beyond.” 
“Having access to health care can make the transition to adulthood easier for former foster youth,” said Rep. Bacon. “Without a traditional support system, foster youth face an increased risk of chronic illness and need for mental health and dental care. Ensuring that former foster youth are eligible for Medicaid and have access to dental services helps prevent them from falling through the cracks. I’m pleased to co-lead this package with Rep. Kamlager-Dove to strengthen support for young people as they transition out of foster care.” 
The bipartisan Congressional Caucus on Foster Youth provides a forum for Members of Congress to discuss and develop policy recommendations to strengthen the child welfare system and improve the overall well-being of youth and families. The Foster Youth Caucus is committed to ensuring that our nation's vulnerable, yet resilient, youth are provided with the opportunities and support necessary to succeed. 
# # #
title: Kamlager-Dove, Bacon Reintroduce Bipartisan Bills to Expand Medicaid Eligibility for Foster Youth

Bonamici, Moore Introduce Bipartisan Bill to Safely Dispose Opioids
WASHINGTON, DC [10/1/26] – Representatives Suzanne Bonamici (D-OR) and Riley M. Moore (R-WV) introduced bipartisan legislation to help people securely and safely dispose of unnecessary prescription medication.
The Safe Disposal of Opioids Act aims to stop prescription drug abuse by establishing a national grant program to install and maintain roughly 10,000 secure disposal receptacles across the country. These drop boxes will be conveniently located throughout healthcare facilities and community pharmacies where patients pick up their prescriptions, providing an easy way to dispose of excess medication.
"Providing a safe, easy way to get rid of unused medication is something we can do right now to protect families and neighbors across Oregon and the country," said Congresswoman Suzanne Bonamici. "When people have a convenient place in their community to drop off leftover opioids, it keeps medication out of the wrong hands, reduces the risk of abuse, and gives everyone peace of mind. This bipartisan legislation will make a real difference in keeping homes and neighborhoods safe."
“The dangerous scourge of opioids has devastated communities across West Virginia, more than anywhere else across the country,” said Congressman Riley M. Moore. “We must do everything we can to keep these deadly drugs off our streets and prevent unused opioids from being diverted for abuse. I’m proud to be the Republican leader on the Safe Disposal of Opioids Act, and I support commonsense solutions that help protect our families and communities.”
The grant program is funded through a fee imposed on pharmaceutical manufacturers that produce opioids. The legislation includes a rebate program to prevent the cost from being passed on to patients in hospice or with cancer who rely on opioid medication for pain management.
The Safe Disposal of Opioids Act legislative text can be viewed here.
Bonamici first introduced this bipartisan bill in 2018 based on feedback she got while hosting a series of community discussions about the opioid crisis in NW Oregon.

title: Bonamici, Moore Introduce Bipartisan Bill to Safely Dispose Opioids

Washington, D.C. — Today, Congresswoman Marilyn Strickland (WA-10) and Congressman David P. Joyce (OH-14) introduced a bipartisan Multigenerational HOMES (Housing Opportunities for Modifying Existing Structures) Act. The bill is one of a kind in that it will provide a tax credit for homeowners who renovate their homes to accommodate an elderly family member, a family member with a disability, or a family member who will be a live-in caregiver.

“This bill helps keep families under one roof at all stages of life if they choose to care for their aging family members,” said Strickland. “The tax credit provides families with additional in-home care options.”

“As a member of the Congressional Assisting Caregivers Today Caucus, I know how important it is to give families the flexibility to provide care without leaving the homes and communities they know,” said Congressman Joyce. “The Multigenerational HOMES Act would help families adapt their existing homes to meet their changing needs, making it easier for loved ones to live together while making better use of our existing housing stock. By giving families more options to share a home and care for one another, we can reduce the costs and pressures of finding additional housing while empowering families to make the decisions that work best for them.”

The tax credit can be used to make renovations such as adding handrails, stairlifts, wider doorways, and separate entrances. This makes it more affordable for families who choose the option of in-home caregiving for aging relatives.

“NAHB commends Rep. Strickland for introducing legislation to help families remain in their homes. The Multigenerational HOMES Act would provide a tax credit for homeowners to make renovations that accommodate family members with accessibility needs or disabilities. Caregivers face many challenges, and supporting their ability to keep loved ones together under one roof is both important and beneficial,” said Bill Owens, Chairman, National Association of Home Builders.

“Families live and care across generations, even when our homes and public systems are not designed that way. The Multigenerational HOMES Act would help families create safer, more accessible homes where older adults, people with disabilities, caregivers, and loved ones of every age can remain connected and supported. This is prevention through connection – and a practical investment in family stability, independence, and dignity,” said Kristen Kiefer, Executive Director, Generations United.

The legislation is endorsed by: AARP, Generations United, the National Association of Home Builders, and the National Association of the Remodeling Industry.

###
title: Strickland Introduces Bipartisan Intergenerational Housing Bill

Washington, D.C. – Today, U.S. Representatives Norma Torres (CA-35) and Chuck Fleischmann (TN-03) introduce a bipartisan resolution recognizing October 2, 2026, the first Friday of October, as National Manufacturing Day.

The resolution celebrates the important role American manufacturing plays in strengthening the economy, driving innovation, supporting supply chains, and creating good-paying, family-sustaining jobs in communities across the country.

“Supporting the Manufacturing industry is key to growing the Inland Empire’s economy and creating pathways to good-paying careers in our region,” said Congresswoman Norma Torres. “Every year, I have the opportunity to visit manufacturers across my district and see firsthand the innovation, skill, and hard work that keep our economy moving. Manufacturing Day is an opportunity to recognize these workers and businesses while encouraging the next generation to explore careers in this growing industry. I am proud to once again partner with Congressman Fleischmann to celebrate American manufacturing and the people who make it possible.”

"Whether it’s the cars we drive, the homes we live in, or the products we use every day, manufacturing touches every part of our lives. It creates good jobs, helps our communities thrive, and gives workers the chance to build new skills and brighter futures. That’s why it’s so important to take a moment to celebrate the people behind America’s manufacturing industry. I’m proud to work with my colleagues on this bipartisan resolution. I will always stand up for American manufacturing in Congress,” said Congressman Fleischmann.

Manufacturers contribute approximately $2.9 trillion to the U.S. economy, accounting for roughly 11 percent of gross domestic product. Nearly 12.9 million Americans are directly employed in manufacturing, with millions more jobs supported throughout supply chains and related industries. American manufacturers are also major drivers of innovation, investing hundreds of billions of dollars in research and development.

Congresswoman Torres has made supporting manufacturers and developing a skilled workforce a priority in the Inland Empire. Through her annual “Made in the 35th” manufacturing tour, Torres visits local manufacturers to hear directly from employers and workers about their needs, highlight locally made products, and promote career opportunities in the industry.

Torres and Fleischmann have also worked together to strengthen American manufacturing and supply chains. Their bipartisan National MEP Supply Chain Database Act was included in the CHIPS and Science Act (Public Law No: 117-167) to help manufacturers better prepare for and respond to future supply chain disruptions.

Report Responds to Congressional Request for Information on Regulatory, Ethical, and Cultural Considerations for Integrating Prescription Psychedelic Medicine into the United States

Washington, DC — The Congressional Psychedelics Advancing Therapies (PATH) Caucus released a report capturing responses to a 2024 Request for Information into how psychedelic-assisted therapy (PAT) could be safely and ethically integrated into the United States health care system.

The report found broad consensus among clinicians, researchers, veteran advocates, Tribal leaders, payors, regulators, and patients that PAT could offer safe, equitable, and evidence-based treatment for a wide array of treatment-resistant conditions – including generalized anxiety disorder, depression, PTSD, and substance use disorder. It also offered several federal policy recommendations for the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and Congress to consider as they aim to improve health outcomes for patients across the country.

“Every day, more than 130 Americans die by suicide, including over 20 veterans,” said Congressman Lou Correa (D-CA-46). “Psychedelic-assisted therapy has shown promising results for treatment, but we need more information. This report is a serious step toward bringing it into our health care system safely and ethically, so that all Americans, especially those who served our country, can get care that works for them.”

“This report is exactly the kind of resource Congress needs to legislate responsibly,” ?said?Congressman Jack Bergman (R-MI-01).?“Our Veterans have waited long enough for successful treatments and breakthrough therapies to help mitigate PTSD and other service-related conditions. It’s time to advance real, actionable policies that meet the unmet mental and physical health needs of Americans in every community.”?

Key Findings

Respondents agree that the U.S. faces a severe mental and behavioral health crisis – including treatment-resistant depression, PTSD, suicidality, substance use disorder, and high unmet needs among veterans, terminally ill patients, minorities, low-income families, seniors, and rural communities – requiring novel and efficacious treatments.

Respondents highlight clinical trial evidence suggesting that PAT can produce meaningful and sometimes transformative improvements in PTSD, depression, end-of-life distress, addiction, and overall functioning and quality of life, though it is not considered a single solution and is seen as appropriate only in structured, supervised medical settings.

Respondents encourage national guidance and credential verification systems to be developed before the first FDA approvals of prescription psychedelic medicines.

Respondents highlight the need for evidence-based, standardized adverse event monitoring and robust ethical guidelines to protect patients and ensure trust.

Respondents recommend federal guidance that supports multidisciplinary, culturally competent care teams.

Policy Recommendations

The report suggests that federal agencies – including the FDA, U.S. National Institutes of Health, Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, Department of Homeland Security, Department of Veterans Affairs, Department of Defense, Drug Enforcement Administration, and Office of National Drug Control Policy –

should work with state regulators and Tribal Nations/Territories to develop national guidelines for safe and ethical delivery of prescription psychedelic medicines

The report recommends that federal agencies establish flexible, tiered credentialing pathways to balance safety with accessibility, and to standardize consent and screening protocols nationally.

The report proposes a hybrid policy framework to guide Congress, federal agencies, Tribal Nations/Territories, states, and communities in a balanced, pragmatic rollout of PAT, supported by coordinated leadership, flexible regulation, investment in workforce and infrastructure, and robust long-term data systems.

See here for the full report.

About the Congressional PATH Caucus

The bipartisan Congressional Psychedelics Advancing Therapies (PATH) Caucus, co-chaired by Representatives Jack Bergman (R-MI) and Lou Correa (D-CA), aims to address the nation’s mental health crisis by promoting rigorous, FDA-aligned clinical research into the therapeutic potential of psychedelic-assisted treatments for mental health disorders and integrating these promising treatments into the U.S. health care system for millions of patients with unmet needs.
title: Congressional PATH Caucus Releases Report Outlining Recommendations for Safe Integration of Psychedelic-Assisted Therapy

WASHINGTON, D.C – Today, Representative Chrissy Houlahan (PA-06), with Representative Marilyn Strickland (WA-10) and Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), led the bicameral introduction of the Military Officer Promotion Integrity Act to protect qualified military officers from being arbitrarily removed from promotion consideration for ideological or political reasons, by establishing clear standards, basic due process, and meaningful independent review.

“For the last year and a half, Secretary Hegseth has systematically damaged and undermined the previously unbiased military promotion system, and he has done so under the nose of the President, who reportedly has little to no awareness of Secretary Hegseth’s destructive purge of our military talent and leadership,” said Rep. Houlahan. “Today, we ensure that at least Congress will know when the Secretary tries to strike exceptionally qualified military officers from promotion slates – and we can take action to stop the removal. Once again, fairness, transparency, and objectivity will determine which officer has earned their next rank, and not their allegiance to the political whims of Secretary Hegseth.”

“Secretary Hegseth continues to deny promotions to our most qualified military officials,” said Rep. Strickland. “This bill allows Congress to intervene when a military official is denied or slated to be removed from a rightfully earned promotion.”

“Ironically, no one spends more time obsessing over gender and race than Secretary Hegseth, who is relentlessly blocking promotions and purging the military ranks of women, minorities, and anyone who fails to watch as much Fox News as he does,” said Rep. Blumenthal. “If Secretary Hegseth is really committed to meritocracy, he should fully support this legislation to prevent political meddling in military promotions. His disgraceful promotions decisions are only one piece of a much broader and deeply dangerous effort to politicize our military and undermine its proud tradition of nonpartisan service.”

The legislation is co-sponsored in the Senate by Senators Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), Jacky Rosen (D-NV), and Mazie K. Hirono (D-HI). The bill is endorsed by VoteVets, Protect Democracy, the National Women’s Law Clinic (NWLC), and Retired Major General Steve Lepper, co-founder of the Former JAG Working Group.

“Military officers earn their promotions through years of service, sacrifice, and proven leadership. Pulling them from consideration because of politics not only derails careers, but it tells every officer and every American that fealty matters more than competence. Most important is our oath to support and defend the U.S. Constitution, against all enemies, foreign and domestic. The Military Officer Promotion Integrity Act makes sure that these decisions rest only on facts. VoteVets applauds Senator Blumenthal’s leadership and we call on Congress to pass this critical bill without delay,” said Retired Major General Paul Eaton, VoteVets Senior Advisor.

“A nonpartisan, merit-based military promotion system is crucial to military readiness. It ensures our senior ranks are filled by officers who have demonstrated the expertise and leadership that our readiness depends on. This legislation strengthens the promotion process, reinforces our operational edge, and sustains the confidence of the American people in their military,” said Zachary West with Protect Democracy.

“Our country and our nation’s service members deserve a promotion system that is based on merit and leadership skills—not one that can be abused to single out and block individuals because of their sex, race or support for diversity, equity and inclusion,” said Gaylynn Burrough, vice president for education and workplace justice at the National Women’s Law Center Action Fund. “Pete Hegseth’s unprecedented and outrageous interference in the promotions of women and people of color in the military is an affront to our nation’s ideals of nondiscrimination and equal opportunity and shows his willingness to put ideology over national security. We are grateful that Senator Blumenthal is taking action to address these senseless actions through Military Officer Promotion Integrity Act of 2026.”

“The United States military’s decisive advantage has always been the quality of its leaders. That’s why the officer promotion processes of each Service are so important. In recent months, individual officers selected for promotion based on their skills, experience, and leadership potential have been removed without explanation by individual senior leaders. Not only are such removals unfair to the removed officers, they undermine the confidence all officers must have in a system so crucial to their career progression and to America’s national security,” said Retired Major General Steve Lepper, co-founder of the Former JAG Working Group. “Senator Blumenthal’s legislation addresses these concerns by establishing minimum fairness standards whenever an officer is removed from a promotion list. If enacted, these standards will provide removed officers opportunities to challenge their removal and will subject the process to necessary congressional oversight. If enacted, this legislation will hopefully restore the fairness, transparency, and confidence needed to ensure America’s military preserves its competitive leadership advantage.”

The full text of the bill is available here.
title: Reps. Houlahan, Strickland, Sen. Blumenthal Introduce Bicameral Legislation to Depoliticize Military Promotions

PITTSBURGH, PA – October 1, 2026 — Today, Congresswoman Summer L. Lee (PA-12) and Congressman Chris Deluzio (PA-17) announced $11,023,181 in federal funding to upgrade thousands of feet of lighting and pavement on Runway 10L/28R at the Pittsburgh International Airport (PIT), further modernizing Western Pennsylvanians’ go-to airport.

The U.S. Department of Transportation awards this money through the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). The multi-phase funding will help extend the service life of the runway, minimize Foreign Object Debris (FOD), improve aircrafts’ ride quality, and make the airfield safer at Pittsburgh International Airport.

“Pittsburgh International Airport is one of the gateways to Western Pennsylvania, and the infrastructure behind it has to be safe, reliable, and ready for the people and workers who depend on it every single day,” said Congresswoman Lee. “This more than $11 million federal investment is exactly what public dollars should be doing: coming back home, strengthening the things our communities rely on, supporting good jobs, and making sure a major piece of our regional economy is built to last. I’m glad to see this funding headed home to Pittsburgh International Airport, and I’ll keep fighting to bring federal investment back to Western Pennsylvania.”

“We in Western Pennsylvanians should be able to rely on the safety and reliability of our infrastructure,” said Congressman Deluzio. “That’s why I am excited to announce another round of federal funding that will help make the Pittsburgh Airport one of the safest and most modern airports in the world.”

“Airports across the country are part of national critical infrastructure and federal support is key in helping to keep the national airspace moving. Pittsburgh International Airport is an important economic driver for our region and this grant helps to fund airfield improvements at PIT including runway paving and upgrading lighting infrastructure. Thank you to Congressman Deluzio and our entire federal delegation for their continued support,” said Pittsburgh International Airport CEO Christina Cassotis.
title: Reps. Lee, Deluzio Announce $11 Million More in Federal Funding for Safety Upgrades at Pittsburgh Airport
